title: The Merchant and Mrs. Caton
premise: Three days after Arthur Caton's mysterious death in a New York hotel, Prairie Avenue is whispering about his widow Delia and the wealthiest merchant in Chicago, whose mansion stands just across the alley.

opening.text:
JAUNT: THE MERCHANT AND MRS. CATON. Monday morning, 21 November 1904. A telegram has arrived from New York, and the blinds are drawn in a house on Calumet Avenue.

Four stops, on foot, from the widow's door, through the rear yards the servants share, to the front steps of Marshall Field, the merchant prince of Chicago. Everyone on Prairie Avenue knows this story, and no one acknowledges it aloud. Thirty years of dinners, transatlantic voyages and rumors are approaching their conclusion, and this morning the only people openly discussing it are the ones who carry the coal.

Begin on Calumet Avenue, at the house with the drawn blinds.

stops.text: Calumet Avenue, behind Prairie, beside the Caton house, its blinds drawn. On Friday, 18 November, Arthur J. Caton died at New York's Waldorf-Astoria hotel, and the cause remains uncertain: "Some said he succumbed to liver failure. Others ascribed the demise to peritonitis". A newspaper in Ottawa, Illinois, will insinuate that he took his own life. He was the son of Judge John Dean Caton, one of the state's first chief justices, and a lawyer, sportsman and clubman who bred horses and dogs on the family farm. His wife Delia, a hardware heiress he married in 1876, hosted the most celebrated parties in Chicago. They had no children. This morning there is a widow, and the news is traveling from the house to the stable. Proceed around the back, to the yards between Calumet and Prairie.

stage.caption: In the Caton side yard a maid carries the news to the coachman, who removes his hat, while the groom halts his work at the coach house door.

cast.name: A maid of the Caton house (no card in the town; an unnamed figure)
The Caton coachman (no card in the town; an unnamed figure)
A Caton groom (no card in the town; an unnamed figure)

stops.text: The back yards, where Calumet meets Prairie at the rear fence. Turn around and the Field house is immediately before you, its coach house on the alley. The servants of both households have shared this ground for years and have absorbed every rumor. Arthur Meeker, who grew up on this street, recorded the most extravagant: "it was even absurdly asserted that an underground tunnel connected the Caton house on Calumet with the Field house on Prairie". Meeker dismissed it as absurd, and it was. Yet a society diarist noted that "Delia sometimes traveled to Europe with Marshall Field without Arthur accompanying them". Now Arthur is dead, Field has been a widower for eight years, and a laundress from the Field house is leaning on the fence. Continue to Prairie Avenue and find the man himself.

stage.caption: Karolina Hall crosses from the Field yard to the fence, where a Caton maid waits with the news.

cast.name: A Caton laundress (no card in the town; an unnamed figure)

stops.text: 1905 Prairie, the Marshall Field mansion, constructed in 1876 for roughly $2 million and "the first in Chicago to be completely wired for electricity". Field is the most powerful businessman in the city. Decades ago he proposed to his first wife by leaping aboard her departing train; one account claims that "Mrs. Field led Marshall Field a hell-on-earth life", and Nannie Field died in France in 1896. Meeker stated the remainder bluntly: "he fell in love with his friend's wife years before he was able to marry her", and "in the Nineties, divorce was unthinkable: they had to wait for him (Arthur Caton) to die, which, distressingly, he didn't do until 1904". That was Friday. Thomas Benson, the Irish-born butler, attends the door; John Dunford, the English coachman, approaches from the stable. The mansion will be demolished in 1955.

stage.caption: Marshall Field emerges from his door and pauses on the steps to gaze east, toward Calumet Avenue, before his coachman reaches him.

stops.text: From farther up the street, the Field house resembles any other on the row; it is not. Field disliked public speaking, and one evening, at one of the Catons' lavish dinners, he was called upon to say a few words. Delia leapt to her feet and answered on his behalf: "Mr. Field just wants me to remind you that the White Sale starts next Monday". It was a joke about his department store, delivered by another man's wife at her husband's own table, and the guests who repeated it afterward described it as the evening everyone recognized how intimate those two had become. The ladies passing the Field house this morning carefully avoid looking at it, and they are discussing nothing else. Arthur Caton is not yet buried; everyone can predict what follows, and nobody dares to say it.

stage.caption: Two ladies of the avenue stroll past the Field house with their heads together, deliberately not looking at it.

cast.name: A second lady of the street (unnamed)

legs.story: Through the gap to the rear yards, with the Caton fence on one side and Marshall Field's coach house on the other.
Around by the side path to Prairie Avenue and the façade of 1905, the house at the center of the gossip.
North along the sidewalk to look back at the Field house as the neighbors do.

endings.text: The walk ends here. They waited less than a year. In 1905 they married at St. Margaret's, Westminster, in London; the license recorded Delia as forty-six and Field as seventy, and "the ceremony was quiet, and attended only by a few friends". They returned to Chicago as husband and wife, and in January 1906 Marshall Field died of pneumonia, contracted on a New Year's Day golf course in a foursome that included Robert Todd Lincoln. After three decades of waiting, they had a few months together. Delia inherited $1 million and the Prairie Avenue mansion, relocated to Washington, where her residence became known as the Pink Palace, and lived until 1937.

keepsake.title: A Widow's Calling Card
keepsake.text: An interpretive card of the Caton and Field households in November 1904; a reconstruction for this walk, not a historical artifact.

evidence.text: Arthur J. Caton died 'November 18, 1904, at New York's Waldorf-Astoria hotel'. 'The cause of death was inexact. Some said he succumbed to liver failure. Others ascribed the demise to peritonitis.' An Ottawa, Illinois Times story suggested he may have taken his own life.

Delia Spencer, the daughter of one of the founders of the Hibbard, Spencer & Bartlett hardware firm, married Arthur Caton in 1876. He was the son of Judge John Dean Caton, one of Illinois' first chief justices; a lawyer, sportsman and clubman, he loved golf and polo and bred horses and dogs on the family's Ottawa farm.
evidence.locator: Other Mrs. Field: the paragraphs on Delia and the Catons; Second Mrs. Field: 'Delia Spencer married Arthur Caton in 1876.'

evidence.text: Arthur Meeker's mother 'always declared that nobody ever gave such wonderful parties as Delia Caton'. The Catons had no children and entertained in 'their big, elaborate house on Calumet Avenue'.
evidence.locator: The paragraph quoting Meeker on the Catons' entertaining.

evidence.text: The Merchant and Mrs. Caton: the day, Monday 21 November 1904, the hour and the order of the walk are this jaunt's framing, chosen because the stories meet on it (three days after Arthur Caton's death, a Monday of the Reading Class, before Kimball's death in December). No visit on that day is asserted.

The Merchant and Mrs. Caton: who is seen at each stop, where they stand, what they do and when are reconstructed. People with cards in the town play themselves; people the town has no card for (and the unnamed servants, callers and passers-by) are unnamed figures in period dress, and no likeness is claimed. No word anyone says is asserted.

Arthur Meeker: 'The gossip of the day cast the worst light on the affair; it was even absurdly asserted that an underground tunnel connected the Caton house on Calumet with the Field house on Prairie, which was just in front of it, or just back.'
evidence.locator: Second Mrs. Field: the Meeker paragraph; Other Mrs. Field: the Beveridge Chronicle's 'subterranean tunnel'.

evidence.text: There were rumours that Field and Delia Caton were lovers for nearly 30 years, and 'Delia sometimes traveled to Europe with Marshall Field without Arthur accompanying them.'
evidence.locator: The paragraph quoting The Chronicle of Catherine Eddy Beveridge.

evidence.text: Field proposed to Nannie Douglas Scott by jumping aboard her train as it left Chicago; he got off at the next stop and walked back to work. Their marriage foundered: by Longstreet's account 'Mrs. Field led Marshall Field a hell-on-earth life'. Nannie took to the South of France, and died in France in 1896.
evidence.locator: The post's opening paragraphs and the paragraph on Nannie's death.

evidence.text: The census of 1 June 1900 enumerated John Dunford, coachman, born in England, as the head of his own household in the rear building behind 1905 Prairie, and Thomas Benson, butler, born in Ireland, in the house.

Marshall and Nannie Field had three children: Louis, who died in infancy, and Marshall, Jr. and Ethel, raised at 1905 Prairie, 'the first in Chicago to be completely wired for electricity', built in 1876 at a cost of some $2 million.

Meeker: 'he fell in love with his friend's wife years before he was able to marry her.' And: 'In the Nineties, divorce was unthinkable: they had to wait for him (Arthur Caton) to die, which, distressingly, he didn't do until 1904.'
Marshall Field Residence, 1905 S. Prairie Avenue: later converted to an aeronautical university. Razed 1955.

Marshall Field: 'Give the lady what she wants'; 'the wealthiest and most powerful businessman in Chicago', his fortune valued at $125 million in 1905. His son Marshall Field Jr. was shot on 22 November 1905; Field himself died of pneumonia on 16 January 1906, caught after a New Year's Day golf game with, among others, Robert Todd Lincoln.
evidence.locator: The biography's paragraphs on the store, his wealth, his son and his death.

evidence.text: Field was reluctant to make a speech at one of the Catons' grand dinners, and Delia sprang to her feet and said: Mr. Field just wants me to remind you that the White Sale starts next Monday.
evidence.locator: The paragraph quoting Meeker, Chicago, With Love.

evidence.text: The marriage licence acquired in London in 1905 gave Delia as 46 and Field as 70. They married at St. Margaret's, Westminster; 'The ceremony was quiet, and attended only by a few friends.' Field died in 1906 of pneumonia after a round of golf in a foursome that included Robert Todd Lincoln. Delia was left $1 million and the Field mansion on Prairie Avenue, moved to Washington, D.C., where her house was known as the Pink Palace, and died in 1937.
evidence.locator: Second Mrs. Field: the paragraphs on the marriage and after; Wikipedia: the death on 16 January 1906.
